newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada set to decide on murdered stowaways case.
newsitem.headline: Canada set to decide on murdered stowaways case.

text.p: A judge will decide on Thursday if there is enough evidence to try six Taiwanese sailors accused of killing three Romanian stowaways at sea in what has become an international diplomatic tussle.
If Nova Scotia Supreme Court Justice Michael MacDonald finds there is sufficient evidence for a trial, Canadian Justice Minister Allan Rock must then decide whether to extradite the men to Romania.
Romania and Taiwan are wrangling for control of the Taiwanese officers' fate. China, claiming sovereignty over Taiwan, argues that it has jurisdiction over the seamen.
Cheng Shiou, 34, captain of the merchant ship involved, the Maersk Dubai, has denied any wrongdoing by him or his officers.
The accused officers declined comment to reporters, but their translator, Huey-Jean Yang, told Reuters the men "feel like chess pieces being played in an international power struggle."
The tangled tale began last May when eight Filipino crewmen deserted the container ship Maersk Dubai in this port city on Canada's Atlantic coast.

The distraught crewmen told Canadian port authorities that the ship's Taiwanese officers had ordered two Romanian stowaways onto a makeshift raft off the Spanish coast in March. The Filipinos said another Romanian discovered on the ship during a separate voyage in May was also forced overboard in the mid-Atlantic.
A fourth Romanian, Nicolae Pasca, survived with the help of the Filipinos, who said they hid him in the bowels of the ship, bringing him food and clothing.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police stormed the ship, arrested the officers and charged them with first-degree murder on behalf of Romania.
The Filipinos' testimony painted a harrowing, but inconsistent picture of stowaways murdered to avoid paying Canadian fines for harboring illegal immigrants.

The alleged murder victims, Radu Danciu, 29, and Petre Sangeorzan, 20, pleaded with the ship's officers for their lives, the Filipinos said. The third stowaway, Gheorghe Mihoc, 18, was thrown into the sea on another voyage two months later, the crewmen testified.

Complicating the case, surviving stowaway Pasca testified that he never saw the other Romanians on the Maersk Dubai. The bodies of the alleged victims were never found and Romanian investigators said the missing men's families had not heard from them.
Taipei argues that since the Maersk Dubai sailed under the Taiwanese flag it has jurisdiction over the accused men under United Nations maritime treaties.

Romania based its extradition request on an 1893 treaty between Britain and Romania, which Romania says applies to Canada as part of the Commonwealth. Bucharest is also relying on an obscure precedent in international law stipulating that an accused person can be tried in the crime victim's homeland.
Defense lawyers for the six officers argued in court last autumn that Canada did not have the jurisdiction to extradite the men to Romania to face murder charges.

James Martin, a Canadian prosecutor representing the Romanian government, contended that Justice MacDonald needed only to determine if there was sufficient evidence to commit the men to trial. Canada would then decide if they should be extradited, he said.
